description: TEVAN - Tactical EVA Navigator . A helmet navigator for astronauts on a Mars mission, built for NASA Space Apps 2026 ("Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map"). The screen is the inside of the helmet: you see Jezero Crater through a curved visor, and TEVAN draws on the glass.
summary:
TEVAN (Tactical EVA Navigator)

On Mars, an astronaut’s health risk depends on where they walk. Radiation, steep slopes and distance from shelter all change with the terrain. TEVAN is built on that idea. It combines a tactical map, a health model and a route engine into one helmet-visor navigator, to make Marswalks measurably safer.

TEVAN runs in the browser and uses real NASA and USGS data for Jezero Crater. That includes elevation, slope, high-resolution orbital images, Perseverance’s landing site and its actual drive path. Astronauts plan routes on a map that works like Google Maps, with zoom, search, place cards and custom labels. For each route, TEVAN works out the distance, elevation gain, steepest slope and travel time. It then forecasts heart rate, oxygen use, fatigue and radiation dose. When fatigue passes a safe limit, TEVAN suggests a safer route on its own and explains why.

Inside the curved visor display, a webcam follows the astronaut’s gaze. Looking at a boulder, site or crewmate brings up a mixed-reality info card that stays for 3.5 seconds, even after they turn away. Voice control works out what the astronaut means, even with accents or misheard words. A scout drone uncovers unexplored terrain, and live Perseverance photos show what the rover sees.
details:
What it does and how it works
TEVAN (Tactical EVA Navigator) is built on one idea: on Mars, an astronaut's health risk depends on geography. TEVAN combines a tactical map, a health model and a route engine into one helmet-visor navigator for Marswalks (EVAs). It shows real Jezero Crater terrain from NASA and USGS sources, including elevation, slope, high-resolution orbital images, Perseverance's landing site and its actual drive path. Astronauts plan routes on a map that works like Google Maps, with zoom, search, place cards and labels. For each route, TEVAN calculates the distance, elevation gain, steepest slope and time. It then forecasts heart rate, oxygen use, fatigue and radiation dose. If fatigue crosses a safe limit, TEVAN suggests a safer route on its own and explains why.

Benefits and impact
Astronauts can see how a route will affect their body before they walk it. That lowers the risk of exhaustion, radiation overexposure and dangerous slopes, and it shows that EVA safety can be planned and measured. The same approach could support future crewed missions and training on Earth.

Tools
TypeScript, Vite and Three.js for the 3D visor, deployed on Netlify. In-browser speech recognition and webcam gaze tracking. NASA Trek and USGS Astrogeology data, plus Perseverance raw images. Python to convert GeoTIFF terrain data. Stitch AI for UI design and Suno for audio.

Creativity
A curved helmet HUD replaces a dashboard. Looking at a boulder or crewmate brings up a mixed-reality card that stays for 3.5 seconds, even after the astronaut turns away. Voice control works out what the astronaut means, even with accents. A scout drone uncovers unexplored terrain, and live rover photos show what Perseverance sees.

Factors we considered
Astronaut workload, keeping the display uncluttered, hands-free control while wearing gloves, real terrain accuracy, working offline with backup data, and running in a normal browser (Chrome or Edge) with no special hardware.
